conversation.content:
Good morning — I’m so glad you’re here. My name is Maya Patel, and I’m the perinatal mental-health clinician who works with new moms. I’ll be guiding you through a short, well-trusted questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It was designed to help us understand how you’ve been feeling in the past week so we can make sure you’re getting the right support now that your baby is here.

Everything we discuss stays between us unless you tell me you’re in immediate danger; then we’d talk together about the safest next steps. There are only ten questions, and I’ll ask each one conversationally — no need to remember numbers or categories. If any question feels hard to answer, just say what feels closest. We’ll take it at your pace, and you can pause any time.

Ready?  
Here’s the first one:

Over the past seven days, have you still been able to look forward to things you used to enjoy — like seeing a friend, listening to music, or getting outside — or has that felt pretty flat or absent?

I still look forward to some things—like when my sister drops by with coffee or when I get twenty minutes to scroll through my playlist—but it’s not the same spark I used to have. Most of the time it feels kind of “meh,” like I’m going through the motions more than actually enjoying it.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah, I can still laugh—especially when my husband sends those silly memes or when the baby makes those little milk-drunk faces—but it takes more effort than before. It’s like the laughter doesn’t come as naturally; I have to remind myself it’s okay to find things funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do look forward to some stuff—like when Mom brings dinner or when I get a quiet minute to sip my coffee while the baby naps—but the excitement feels kind of muted. It’s more “oh, that’ll be nice” instead of the real buzz I used to feel.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Yesterday the baby was fussy for an hour and I kept thinking maybe I ate something that upset her, or that I’m just not soothing her right. I know babies cry, but the little voice in my head still says, “You should’ve figured it out by now.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

I do get those waves of worry—like last night I suddenly thought her breathing sounded weird even though she was fine. It hits out of nowhere and my heart races, but it usually passes if I get up and peek at her or do a quick diaper check.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Once or twice I’ve had that sudden tight-chest feeling—like yesterday when I was folding laundry and my mind just jumped to “what if she stops breathing in her sleep?” It felt almost like a mini surge of panic, but it eased off after a couple of minutes when I told myself she was right there in the bassinet, perfectly fine.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. When she cluster-feeds or won’t settle, I feel like I’m drowning in tiny tasks—diapers, bottles, texts I haven’t answered. I usually get through it, but I end those days exhausted and snapping at my partner over nothing.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not really. I’ve been tired enough that I can usually fall asleep once the baby’s down—though sometimes my mind keeps ticking through the day’s little “mom fails” and it takes an extra half-hour to drift off.
I have felt sad or miserable
Yeah, I do feel that way some days—like a heavy, gray mood settles in. It’s not all the time, but I’ll catch myself tearing up when I’m rocking her and thinking, “I should be happier than this.”
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I’ve cried a couple of times this week—mostly when I’m alone with her in the late afternoon and everything feels overwhelming. It’s not an all-day thing, but yeah, the tears just start and I can’t always stop them right away.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I might feel low, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 14: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (verbal administration)

Symptoms endorsed:  
- Anhedonia (laugh/pleasure blunted)  
- Low mood, tearfulness ≥2×/week  
- Excessive self-blame/guilt over infant care  
- Unprompted anxiety/worry with physical symptoms (palpitations, chest tightness)  
- Brief nocturnal panic-like surges  
- Feeling overwhelmed, difficulty coping with daily tasks  
- Mild initial insomnia (day-rumination)

Denies: suicidal ideation, self-harm thoughts.

Pattern: Symptoms fluctuate, peak late afternoon/evening; no impairment in basic self-care; infant care maintained with distress.

Screening significance:  
Moderate depressive features plus comorbid postpartum anxiety; no acute safety concerns at present.  
Recommend routine follow-up, psychoeducation, consideration of formal diagnostic interview (DSM-5-TR) and evidence-based intervention as indicated.
